passages.t: The word of God comes to John in the wilderness
passages.happening:
Luke gives the date with great care. It is the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governs Judea. Herod rules Galilee, his brother Philip rules the lands to the north-east, and Lysanias rules Abilene. Annas and Caiaphas hold the high priesthood. Then, “the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness” (verse 2).

John goes through the whole region around the Jordan River, preaching “a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (verse 3). Luke says this is what Isaiah wrote about: a voice calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord’. Valleys will be filled, mountains brought low, crooked roads made straight, “And all humanity will see God's salvation” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Luke names seven rulers, from the emperor in Rome down to the high priests in Jerusalem. That is how ancient writers dated events, by who was in power. Most count Tiberius's fifteenth year as AD 28 or 29; some count it from an earlier start and get about AD 26. Pilate governed Judea from about 26 to 36. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 bears his name. An inscription found at Abila names ‘Lysanias the tetrarch’, a ruler Luke was once thought to have got wrong. A tetrarch was a ruler of part of a kingdom under Rome. The book page tells more.

Then Luke does something striking. After all the great names, the word of God does not come to any of them. It comes to the son of an old priest, out in the desert.

Annas and Caiaphas are both named, though only one man was high priest at a time. Annas had been high priest years before. Caiaphas, his son-in-law, held the office now, but Annas was still a powerful figure (John 18:13).

Repentance means a change of heart and life, turning around. Baptism means washing in water. Jews of the time knew many kinds of ritual washing for being made clean. John's washing was different. It was done once, John did it to people rather than people washing themselves, and it was a sign of turning back to God.
passages.ot:
The quotation is from Isaiah 40:3-5. In Isaiah, the voice calls for a road to be made through the desert so that God can lead his people home from exile in Babylon. Valleys raised, mountains levelled: the way home is made ready. Isaiah 40 begins “Comfort, comfort My people” (Isaiah 40:1).

Matthew and Mark quote only the first line. Luke carries the quotation on to its end: “and all humanity together will see it” (Isaiah 40:5). Salvation for all people is one of Luke's great themes, and he wants Isaiah's ‘all humanity’ heard from the start.

‘The word of God came to’ is the way the Old Testament introduces prophets. Jeremiah's book begins this way (Jeremiah 1:2). Luke is telling his readers that a prophet has appeared again.
passages.hard: Do the dates fit? Luke's list gives an outer frame that historians can check: Tiberius, Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Annas and Caiaphas all fit the late 20s AD, and Lysanias now appears to fit too. The exact year depends on how Tiberius's reign was counted, so Luke's date points to about AD 26 to 29. Combined with Luke's note that Jesus was ‘about thirty’ (verse 23), this is one of the main pieces of evidence for when Jesus' public work began.
passages.asks: God's word passed over the palace and the high priest's house and came to a man in the desert. Where do you expect to hear from God? Sometimes the voice that matters is not the loudest or the most important. And John's message was simple: get ready, because God is coming.

passages.happening:
Crowds come out to be baptized. John does not flatter them. “You brood of vipers,” he says, “who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (verse 7).

He tells them to show their change of heart by the way they live: “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance” (verse 8). And he warns them not to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ God could raise up children for Abraham out of these stones.

The axe is already at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.
passages.hearers:
A brood of vipers is a nest of baby snakes. Picture snakes rushing out of a burning field ahead of the flames. John asks who warned them to run.

Being a child of Abraham was Israel's great pride and comfort. God had made his promise to Abraham and his children. Many felt that belonging to his family was protection enough. John says it is not. God is not short of children. He could make them out of rocks.

Some have noticed that in Hebrew the words for ‘stones’ and ‘children’ sound alike. John may have been making a play on words. But we do not know for sure which language he spoke, so this is only a possibility.

The axe ‘lies ready at the root’. It is not yet swinging. There is still time.

Matthew says John spoke these words to Pharisees and Sadducees (Matthew 3:7). Luke says the crowds. Luke's point is that no one, religious leader or ordinary person, is safe just by belonging to the right group.
passages.ot: The prophets had spoken this way. Isaiah told Israel to “Look to Abraham your father” (Isaiah 51:2), but also said again and again that a fruitless vine would be judged (Isaiah 5:1-7). Malachi warned of a day “burning like a furnace” when “Not a root or branch will be left” to the wicked (Malachi 4:1). John stands in that line.
passages.hard: Is John too harsh? He calls a crowd of people who came to be baptized a nest of snakes. But notice what he wants: not that they go away, but that they change. The warning is fierce because the danger is real and the time is short. Luke goes on to call his message ‘good news’ (verse 18). A warning that saves your life is good news, even when it stings.
passages.asks: John's question cuts deep: what are you relying on? A family, a church, a tradition, a good reputation? None of these is bad. But none of them replaces a life turned toward God. What fruit would show that your faith is real?

passages.happening:
The crowds ask, “What then should we do?” (verse 10). John answers plainly: “Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none, and whoever has food should do the same” (verse 11).

Tax collectors come to be baptized too. “Teacher,” they ask, “what should we do?” He tells them, “Collect no more than you are authorized” (verse 13).

Then some soldiers ask, “And what should we do?” He says, “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” and, “Be content with your wages” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
This passage is found only in Luke. It shows that John's call to repentance was not vague. It meant changes you could see.

A tunic was the long shirt worn next to the skin. Having two meant you had a spare. John asks ordinary people to give the spare away, and to share food the same way.

Tax collectors, in this region, mostly collected tolls and customs on goods moving along roads and through towns. The right to collect was sold to contractors, who paid in advance and then made their living from what they collected. The local men who did the collecting could charge whatever they could get away with. Many Jews hated them as cheats who worked for foreign rulers. John does not tell them to quit. He tells them to be honest.

The soldiers were probably not Roman legion soldiers. Most think they were troops in the service of Herod Antipas or other local rulers, perhaps guarding the tax collectors. Soldiers were badly paid and could easily bully people for money or threaten to accuse them falsely. John does not tell them to leave the army. He tells them not to abuse their power, and to live on their pay.
passages.ot: John's answers sound like the law and the prophets. The law said, “You must not defraud your neighbor or rob him” (Leviticus 19:13). Isaiah said the fasting God wants is “to share your bread with the hungry” and “to clothe the naked when you see him” (Isaiah 58:7). Micah summed it up: “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard: Why didn't John tell the tax collectors and soldiers to give up their jobs? Christians have drawn different lessons. Some say John shows that faith can be lived out in ordinary and even compromised work, by doing it honestly. Others note that this was a first step, and that Jesus would later call some, like Zacchaeus, to much more (19:8). What is clear is that John's repentance had nothing to do with feelings alone. It reached the wallet, the workplace and the weak.
passages.asks: John's answer for each group was different, because each was tempted differently. If you asked John, ‘What should I do?’, what would he say to you? Where does your work or your money give you a chance to take more than your share, or to share more than you have to?

passages.t: One more powerful is coming; John in prison
passages.happening:
The people are full of hope. They wonder whether John might be the Christ, the promised king. John answers them all: “I baptize you with water, but One more powerful than I will come, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (verse 16).

His winnowing fork is in his hand. He will gather the wheat into his barn and burn up the chaff with a fire that never goes out. With many such words, John preaches the good news to the people.

But John also rebukes Herod, the ruler of Galilee, for taking his brother's wife, Herodias, and for all the other evil he has done. So Herod adds one more wrong to the rest. He locks John up in prison.
passages.hearers:
Many Jews were waiting for the Messiah, and a prophet in the desert stirred their hopes. John refuses the title at once.

Untying a master's sandals was the job of a slave. John says he is not good enough even for that.

Winnowing was how farmers cleaned grain. After the stalks were beaten, the farmer tossed the grain into the air with a wooden fork. The wind blew the light husks, the chaff, away, and the heavy grain fell back to be gathered. The chaff was burned. Everyone in a farming village had seen it done.

Herod here is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee. He had married Herodias, who had been his brother's wife. The law of Moses forbade that (Leviticus 18:16). The Jewish historian Josephus also tells of John's arrest by Herod and his death at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea (Antiquities 18.116-119).

Notice the order. Luke tells of John's imprisonment before he tells of Jesus' baptism. He finishes John's story first, then turns the stage to Jesus.
passages.ot:
Fire, in the Old Testament, both cleans and judges. Malachi asked, “But who can endure the day of His coming?” and said the coming one would be “like a refiner's fire” (Malachi 3:2), burning away what is impure. God promised through Joel, “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28). John joins the two: the coming one brings the Spirit, and the fire.

John's courage before Herod recalls Elijah, who stood up to King Ahab and Queen Jezebel (1 Kings 21:17-24).
passages.hard: What does ‘baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire’ mean? Some read it as one gift: the Spirit who purifies like fire, and they see it fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit came with ‘tongues like flames of fire’ (Acts 2:3). Others read two outcomes: the Spirit for those who repent, and the fire of judgment for those who do not, as the next verse about the chaff suggests. Both readings have long histories, and the passage may hold both.
passages.asks: John was popular, and he could have taken the title people wanted to give him. He pointed away from himself instead. And he told the truth to a powerful man, though it cost him his freedom. Where are you tempted to take credit that belongs to Jesus? And where is the truth costly for you to speak?

passages.happening: When all the people are being baptized, Jesus is baptized too. And while he is praying, heaven opens. The Holy Spirit comes down on him “in a bodily form like a dove” (verse 22). A voice comes from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Luke tells the baptism very briefly. He does not even name John here. What he adds is that Jesus was praying. Luke shows Jesus praying at every turning point: here, before choosing the twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), on the mountain where he was transfigured (9:29) and on the cross. Prayer opens heaven.

Luke also says the Spirit came ‘in a bodily form’. He wants readers to know this was not only an inner feeling. Something was seen.

Notice that the Father, the Son and the Spirit are all present: the Son praying, the Spirit coming down, the Father speaking. Christians have long seen here the one God the church later confessed as Trinity.

Matthew tells the same scene and adds John's protest and Jesus' answer (Matthew 3:14-15). Mark and Luke give the voice speaking to Jesus, ‘You are’; Matthew gives it speaking about him, ‘This is’.
passages.ot: The Father's words join two passages. “You are My Son” is what God says to his anointed king in Psalm 2:7. ‘In You I am well pleased’ echoes Isaiah's servant, “My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him” (Isaiah 42:1). King and servant meet in one person. The open heaven answers Isaiah's prayer that God would ‘rend the heavens and come down’ (Isaiah 64:1).
passages.hard: Why was the sinless Jesus baptized with a baptism of repentance? This is answered more fully in the notes on Matthew 3. Christians have given answers that fit together: he obeyed what God asked; he stood with sinners, taking his place among them long before the cross; and he began the work God had promised. What the passage does not mean is that Jesus had sins to confess. Luke's quiet telling, with Jesus praying among ‘all the people’, stresses that he chose to stand where they stood.
passages.asks: The Father called Jesus beloved before he had preached a sermon or done a miracle. Those who belong to Jesus are welcomed into that love too. Do you pray as someone trying to earn God's attention, or as someone already loved? Jesus prayed, and heaven opened.

passages.t: The family line, back to Adam
passages.happening: Jesus is about thirty years old when he begins his work. Luke then gives his family line. Jesus “was regarded as the son of Joseph” (verse 23), and the list runs backwards from Joseph, son of Heli, through more than seventy names: through Zerubbabel, who led the people home from exile; through David and his son Nathan; through Judah, Jacob, Isaac and Abraham; through Noah, Methuselah and Seth; all the way to “the son of Adam, the son of God” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Family records mattered greatly in Israel. They showed which tribe you belonged to and gave you your place among God's people. Priests, for example, had to prove their descent (Ezra 2:61-63).

Luke's list runs the opposite way from Matthew's. Matthew begins with Abraham and goes down to Jesus. Luke starts with Jesus and goes up. And Luke does not stop at Abraham, the father of the Jewish people. He goes all the way to Adam, the father of every human being. Jesus belongs to the whole human family, not only to Israel.

The list ends with ‘the son of God’. Adam had no human father; he came from God. Placed right after the voice at the baptism saying ‘You are My beloved Son’ and just before the testing in the desert, where the devil says ‘If You are the Son of God’ (4:3), the list makes a quiet point. Adam, God's son, failed when tested. Now another Son will be tested.

‘About thirty’ was an age of beginnings in Israel's story. Joseph was thirty when he entered Pharaoh's service (Genesis 41:46). David was thirty when he became king (2 Samuel 5:4). Luke does not draw the link, but his readers might.
passages.ot:
The early part of the list follows the family lines of Genesis 5 and 11 and 1 Chronicles 1 to 3. One name stands out: a second Cainan in verse 36, between Arphaxad and Shelah. He is not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11, but he is in the Greek translation of Genesis that many early Christians used. Most think Luke followed the Greek. Others think a copyist added the name. The oldest copies of Luke disagree on it.

The line through David's son Nathan, not Solomon, is unusual. Nathan is named among David's sons born in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:14).
passages.hard:
Why does Luke's family tree differ from Matthew's? From Abraham to David the two lists mostly agree. After David they part. Matthew's line runs through Solomon and the kings of Judah to Jacob, Joseph's father. Luke's runs through Nathan to Heli, Joseph's father.

Christians have answered this in several ways, as the notes on Matthew 1 and Matthew's book page explain. Julius Africanus, in the early 200s, suggested the custom of a brother marrying a dead brother's widow (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), so one son could have a legal father and a natural father. Many since the Reformation have held that Luke gives Mary's line, with Heli as Mary's father and Joseph counted as his son by marriage. Others say Matthew traces the royal right to David's throne, and Luke the actual descent. Many modern scholars think the two lists came from different family traditions and cannot be fully joined. The site does not choose among these.

Notice also Luke's careful words: Jesus was ‘regarded as’ the son of Joseph. Luke has already told of the virgin conception (1:34-35). Joseph was Jesus' father in law and in love, but not by nature.
passages.asks: A list of names can feel dull. But every name was a life, and most of them are forgotten except here. Luke traces them all to God. Whoever your family is, and whatever it has been, you too come from Adam and from God. And the one at the top of this list came to belong to every family, yours included.
